title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in Albuquerque, NM: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for Albuquerque national lab, chip plant, structural steel and rail work: Part C choice, Part B travel, eligibility.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Preparation in Albuquerque: Six Days for Inspectors at the National Labs, Rio Rancho, the Steel Erectors and the Railroad
html:
Albuquerque's welding work does not look like an oil town's or a shipyard's. The biggest employers are federal: Sandia National Laboratories and Kirtland Air Force Base on the southeast side, with Los Alamos National Laboratory a couple of hours north. Across the river in Rio Rancho, Intel's chip packaging plant has driven years of heavy construction. A homegrown solar tracker manufacturer has just opened its largest factory, BNSF runs a major rail yard down the valley in Belen, and the metro keeps building schools, hospitals, warehouses and housing under the state's building code. What ties these together for a welding inspector is documentation. Labs, federal contractors and code officials want welds that are qualified, inspected and recorded properly, and the AWS Certified Welding Inspector (CWI) is the credential they recognize.

Atlantis NDT offers a six-day course that prepares Albuquerque-area welders, pipefitters, ironworkers, lab technicians, QC inspectors and engineers for the CWI examination. AWS administers the examination and issues the certification, and every candidate applies to AWS personally and meets its eligibility and vision requirements. Atlantis prepares candidates without any AWS approval or endorsement and without access to exam content. There is no Atlantis classroom in Albuquerque. The course is taken online at your own pace with an instructor answering questions, at an employer's own facility for a group, or one-to-one, online or in person at a location agreed when you book. See the AWS CWI exam prep course page for the outline.

National labs and the base

Sandia sits inside Kirtland Air Force Base on the southeast side of the city. It is run for the National Nuclear Security Administration by National Technology and Engineering Solutions of Sandia, a wholly owned Honeywell subsidiary, and its October 2026 overview put the laboratories' staff at about 16,300, with the headquarters in Albuquerque. Kirtland itself counts more than 22,000 employees, and its latest economic impact statement put the base's fiscal 2024 impact at about seven and a half billion dollars and said it supports about 12 percent of the regional economy. A campus of that size never stops maintaining and replacing mechanical systems, structural steel and specialized test equipment, and the contractors who do that work answer to federal quality requirements that reward careful records.

The labs also employ welding and inspection staff of their own. Los Alamos, for example, keeps a welding chapter in its institutional Engineering Standards Manual, and lab welding work typically comes with inspection documentation, vendor surveillance and, for many positions, a federal security clearance, which generally means US citizenship. Requirements differ by role, so read each listing, but for a candidate in Albuquerque roles like these make the CWI part of a technical career rather than a construction one, often alongside magnetic particle, penetrant and visual testing.

Rio Rancho's chip plant and the construction it brings

Intel has been in Rio Rancho since 1980. In January 2024 it opened Fab 9, a high-volume plant for its Foveros 3D advanced packaging technology, as part of an investment Intel put at three and a half billion dollars, which it said created more than 3,000 construction jobs. Semiconductor plants are welding-heavy buildings to construct and to modify: structural steel for the building and the equipment platforms, process and utility piping, exhaust and chemical distribution systems, and high-purity tubing joined by orbital gas tungsten arc welding. Contractors that build and change these facilities rely on welding inspectors who can work to a demanding owner specification and produce clean records.

Manufacturing and the railroad

Array Technologies, the solar tracker and racking company that was founded and has been headquartered in Albuquerque for more than 35 years, opened a 216,000-square-foot factory in the city in 2026, about three times the size of its previous site, to make in-house components it previously bought from suppliers; the company expects it to support around 300 jobs. Manufacturing growth of that kind brings plant construction, equipment installation and supplier quality work into the city.

About 35 miles south, Belen is what BNSF calls the main fueling and inspection hub on its Southern Transcon between Los Angeles and Chicago, and in 2024 the railroad finished new processing tracks at nearby Becker for fueling, inspections and crew changes. Railcar and locomotive welding has its own AWS code, D15.1, and it is one of the Part C options for the CWI examination, which matters to the small number of local candidates whose careers sit in rail mechanical work.

Building codes and special inspection in New Mexico

New Mexico adopts the International Building Code by rule. The current rule, 14.7.2.8 of the New Mexico Administrative Code, adopts the 2021 IBC with state amendments and took effect on July 14, 2023. The IBC's special inspection chapter applies to structural steel and its welding, which is why structural fabricators, erectors and the testing and inspection firms that serve Albuquerque's commercial, institutional and public projects need welding inspectors who know AWS D1.1. A CWI on a building project checks welder qualifications and procedures, fit-up, preheat on heavier sections, fillet sizes and weld profiles, and records which welds were accepted, repaired or rejected, and those records support the special inspection reports the building official receives.

The ironworkers' apprenticeship is one route into that work. The New Mexico Ironworkers Joint Apprenticeship Committee in Albuquerque trains apprentices in structural erection, the trade that sets, aligns and connects steel members for bolting or welding, and journeymen ironworkers who spend years on erection crews often build exactly the kind of verifiable experience AWS asks for.

Choosing a Part C code in Albuquerque

The CWI's Code Application part is an open-book test on one code chosen at application. AWS D1.1 is the natural choice for structural fabricators, erectors and special inspection firms, and for anyone on building projects across the metro. The ASME option, Section IX with B31.1 and B31.3, suits pipefitters and mechanical contractors on lab, utility and plant piping, and anyone who qualifies welders and procedures for pressure work. AWS D17.1, fusion welding for aerospace applications, fits the few candidates who weld or inspect to aerospace specifications, and D15.1 fits rail mechanical work. AWS D1.5 is the bridge code for those at steel bridge fabricators. Whatever the choice, take the code you will actually use, because the CWI is a working credential and the book becomes a daily reference. Background: AWS D1.1, D1.1 weld acceptance criteria, ASME Section IX and ASME B31.3.

The AWS New Mexico Section

New Mexico members belong to the AWS New Mexico Section in District 20. In January 2026 the section met at Central New Mexico Community College's Smith Brasher Hall in Albuquerque for a visit from an AWS vice president, and it held its general meeting and officer elections in April 2026. Its officers come from Los Alamos National Laboratory, Iron Workers Local 495, the pipefitters of UA Local 412 and an industrial laboratory, which shows the mix of lab, union and inspection people who make up the state's welding community. The section lists a student chapter at Santa Fe Community College, and it set aside its November 2026 meeting for a talk on education opportunities in welding careers. For a CWI candidate, a section meeting is the easiest way to find someone who recently passed and to learn which contractors and labs are hiring.

Where Albuquerque welders train

Central New Mexico Community College offers an Associate of Applied Science in Welding Technology and a Welding Certificate of Completion, covering blueprint reading, mathematics and metallurgy alongside shop work, with options for transferring to a four-year institution. Apprenticeships through the ironworkers' and pipefitters' unions are the other main path, and Santa Fe Community College's trades program sits an hour north. Graduates should remember that AWS counts years of welding-related work, not just schooling: the AWS table lists two years of experience for an associate degree in welding or an engineering field, four for completed trade courses and five for a high school diploma, and AWS decides how a particular program is classed.

Sitting the exam from New Mexico

Each of the three parts needs a score of at least 72 percent. Parts A and C are computer-based tests that you book with Prometric using the eligibility code in your AWS confirmation; Prometric's site will show the closest centers. Part B is the hands-on practical, and AWS runs it only where it holds CWI seminars. The AWS training locations page in November 2026 listed no site in New Mexico; the nearest was Denver, roughly 450 miles north on I-25, with the Texas sites much farther. Most Albuquerque candidates should plan a trip to Denver for Part B and arrange it before booking the computer-based parts. AWS says the practical is usually held on the Saturday or Sunday after a seminar week, with sign-in from 7:30 in the morning and testing starting promptly at 8:00, and examinees must bring a valid driver's license or passport and a copy of the confirmation letter. Driving up the day before is the sensible plan.

What the six days cover, with Albuquerque examples

The first two days build the Fundamentals base: welding processes and their typical defects, terms as AWS A3.0 defines them, joint geometry, welding symbols under AWS A2.4, metallurgy, mechanical and destructive testing, the main NDT methods, fabrication math, safety and the inspector's ethical duties. A pipefitter who has spent years on gas tungsten arc root passes in stainless tubing often finds the symbols and the metallurgy the hardest part, while an engineer from one of the labs may know the metallurgy well and struggle with practical shop terms.

Day three prepares for the practical: reading fillet gauges and a bridge cam gauge, measuring leg size, convexity, reinforcement and undercut, checking misalignment and comparing each reading with the documents supplied. Day four stays inside the chosen code book. For a D1.1 candidate from an erection firm that means prequalified joint details, minimum preheat for thicker members, fillet weld sizes and the visual acceptance table; for an ASME candidate from a mechanical contractor it means Section IX variables and the B31.3 examination and acceptance rules. Day five is timed practice papers for all three parts, and day six returns to the weakest topics and walks through the AWS application, the vision form and exam-day logistics.

Fitting six days around lab and site schedules

Many Albuquerque candidates work on federal sites with strict access rules or on construction projects with long, variable days. The online format avoids both problems: the six-day outline becomes a self-paced study plan with course notes, original practice questions and timed practice papers, studied at home, with an instructor answering questions by message. A fabricator, mechanical contractor or inspection firm with several people preparing can host the corporate format at its own shop or office, where the practical day uses the company's own gauges and weld samples and the code day concentrates on D1.1 or the ASME documents. A candidate who wants personal coaching, or who needs to retake one part, can book the six days one-to-one.

The free NDT practice tests help with the testing questions in Fundamentals, and the Practical NDT welding workshop lets you rehearse visual inspection steps in a browser before the practical.

Eligibility and experience records

AWS sets eligibility in its QC1 specification, combining education with verifiable welding-related experience: one year for a bachelor's degree in welding engineering or welding technology, two for an associate degree in welding, engineering technology, engineering or a physical science, three for engineering or technical courses that count toward a welding bachelor's, four for completed trade or vocational courses and five for a high school diploma, with nine or twelve years for less schooling. Lab technicians and engineers should describe their work in welding terms, naming the processes, materials, codes and inspections involved, because a job title alone tells AWS little. Union journeymen should gather dispatch records or contractor letters that confirm their welding and erection work.

The AWS visual acuity form records near vision of Jaeger J2 at 12 inches or more, with or without glasses, and a color perception test, examined by a qualified eye-care or medical professional close enough to the exam date to meet the AWS time limit. Atlantis does not test vision or confirm experience. The CWI requirements guide covers the rules in more detail.

After the CWI in Albuquerque

Lab and contractor inspection work in this city often calls for magnetic particle, penetrant and visual testing as well as the CWI. Performing those methods needs training and certification by the employer under its written practice. Atlantis provides ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based training in visual testing, magnetic particle testing and penetrant testing, after which the employer certifies the technician. The CWI renews on a nine-year cycle with paperwork at years three and six, and the Senior CWI pathway comes later for inspectors who run programs. Local pages: ultrasonic testing in Albuquerque, magnetic particle inspection in Albuquerque, penetrant testing in Albuquerque and the Practical NDT simulator for Albuquerque.

To get started, tell us the format, the number of candidates, the Part C code each intends to take and an approximate exam month; for an on-site group, include the facility location and weeks that suit your work. We reply within one business day with a quote for that format.

faq.q: Is there an AWS section in Albuquerque?
faq.a: Yes. The AWS New Mexico Section, in District 20, has met at Central New Mexico Community College in Albuquerque, held elections in April 2026 and supports a student chapter at Santa Fe Community College. Use the section finder on aws.org to join.

faq.q: Where do New Mexico candidates take Part B?
faq.a: At a location where AWS holds its CWI seminars. In November 2026 AWS listed none in New Mexico; Denver was the nearest. Fundamentals and Code Application are booked with Prometric after AWS sends your eligibility code.

faq.q: Which Part C code fits Albuquerque work?
faq.a: AWS D1.1 for structural fabrication, erection and special inspection; the ASME option for lab, utility and plant piping; D17.1 for aerospace-specification work; D15.1 for rail mechanical work. Choose the code you will use on the job.

faq.q: Do Los Alamos or Sandia jobs ask for the CWI?
faq.a: It depends on the role. The labs and their construction and maintenance contractors set requirements position by position, and welding inspection roles there may name the CWI, a path toward it, or MT, PT and VT experience. Read each listing.

faq.q: Does New Mexico's building code involve welding inspection?
faq.a: Yes. New Mexico has adopted the 2021 International Building Code by rule, effective July 2023, and the IBC's special inspection chapter covers structural steel and its welding. Firms doing that work need inspectors who know AWS D1.1.

faq.q: I am a journeyman ironworker. How do I document my experience?
faq.a: List each contractor and project with dates, the welding and erection work you did and the codes involved, and collect dispatch records or letters that confirm it. AWS decides what counts; five years apply with a high school diploma.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Albuquerque?
faq.a: No. You can study online at your own pace with instructor support, an employer can host the six days at its own facility, or you can book one-to-one sessions online or in person. Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad.

faq.q: Is the course endorsed by AWS?
faq.a: No. AWS has not approved, accredited or endorsed it, and the practice questions are original. AWS administers the CWI examination and issues the certification.

faq.q: What can I add after the CWI?
faq.a: Visual, magnetic particle and penetrant testing are common additions for lab and fabrication inspectors. Atlantis provides ASNT SNT-TC-1A-based training; see NDT training in Albuquerque. The employer certifies the technician.

faq.q: How do I request a quote?
faq.a: Use the Albuquerque enquiry form with the format, headcount, Part C code and an approximate exam month. We reply within one business day with a quote for that format.
